title: The Overprediction Problem: Aligning Computational Crystal Structure Prediction with Experimental Reality for Two Sulfa Drugs
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society
abstract: Abstract Computational crystal structure prediction (CSP) methods usually overpredict the number of plausible polymorphs. In this study, we used sulfadiazine (SDZ) and sulfamerazine (SMZ), which are respectively monomorphic and pentamorphic (by the end of this study), to investigate the extent of CSP overprediction and its use in designing experiments that identify additional polymorphs. Lattice energy CSP studies (CSP_0) generate a few hundred plausible crystal structures (low-energy minima) for these molecules; however, if these crystal structures are simulated at ambient conditions using a molecular dynamics workflow, then many of the structures can be clustered as equivalent, reducing the number of distinct structures by about 60%. The relative energies are refined using a variety of periodic DFT+D and phonon calculations on the competitive structures. Comparison of the known and CSP-generated thermodynamically competitive structures suggests that forming solid solutions or subliming onto template crystals could enable the discovery of new forms. Solid solutions with the predicted structure of SMZ-IV were found, with SDZ content ranging from 30% to 70%. The combined computation

rubric.why: Central MCSP problem (overprediction) tackled by the Price group with experimental validation of predicted forms; directly relevant to the reader's ranking and landscape work.

summary: Quantifies CSP overprediction for sulfadiazine/sulfamerazine using finite-temperature MD clustering (~60% reduction), DFT+D/phonon reranking, and CSP-guided experiments yielding new solid-solution and templated polymorphs.

title: Diffusion Tree Sampling for Inference Time Adaptation of Crystal Generative Models
abstract: Diffusion-based generative models have become strong priors over plausible crystal structures, but turning that prior into promising candidates requires steering toward several conflicting properties at once. Fine-tuning is expensive and produces a new model for every new objective, while differentiable guidance is not applicable to many real-world tasks. We instead adapt these generative models at inference time using Diffusion Tree Sampling (DTS), a Monte Carlo tree search procedure over the denoising trajectory. We make two technical contributions on top of DTS that are particularly relevant for AI-for-science applications. First, we show how to use existing property-conditional generative models (e.g., models fine-tuned for classifier-free guidance) as guided proposals inside DTS, without distorting the target distribution. Second, we extend DTS to multi-objective sampling, so that a single search produces samples spanning an entire Pareto front. title: Nahual: A Sequence Model for Language and Atoms
abstract: Generative models play a rapidly growing role in the design and simulation of molecules. The most widely used applications of generative models are in large language models (LLMs), owing to the natural flexibility of language for specifying and answering queries. However, generalist LLMs do not effectively handle large sets of 3D coordinates, whereas specialist generative models of 3D molecules cannot reach the controllability afforded by language. To bridge these capabilities, we propose Nahual, a decoder-only autoregressive diffusion model for any sequence of text and 3D molecules. To enable expressive autoregression on continuous coordinates, we propose next-token diffusion, whereby a causal transformer denoises each token while attending to the clean tokens before it, without increasing context size. We train Nahual on a curated set of twelve 3D chemistry tasks ranging from microsolvation to molecular conformer search to adsorption on metal surfaces, with associated evaluation metrics and baselines. title: Kolmogorov-Chapman Maps: Trajectory-Free Learning for Simulating Molecular Dynamics
abstract: Stochastic differential equations (SDEs) describe stochastic processes across a wide range of scientific domains, including physics, biology, and finance. Although individual numerical integration steps are inexpensive, observing meaningful events or transitions can require millions of sequential steps, resulting in substantial wall-clock simulation time and poor hardware utilization. Deep learning offers an alternative by amortizing many integration steps into a single neural network forward pass, potentially enabling much faster simulation. However, existing supervised approaches typically require long simulated trajectory data, which restricts their applicability. In this work, we introduce Kolmogorov-Chapman Maps (KC-Maps), a method for learning the transition kernel of an SDE that relies only on the trajectory-free marginal samples together with the known drift and diffusion coefficients. Given an initial time and state of a process, KC-Maps models its distribution integrated to any given time, corresponding to the weak solution of the SDE. title: Solving Molecular Crystal Structures through Experimental PXRD-Guided Sequential Crystal Structure Prediction
abstract: Structure determination of organic molecular crystals relies heavily on single-crystal X-ray diffraction, yet suitable single crystals are often difficult to obtain. A common alternative uses crystal structure prediction (CSP) to generate candidate structures for subsequent comparison with experimental powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) patterns. Such trial-and-error searches across multiple space groups incur substantial computational costs. Here, we introduce a structure determination protocol that uses experimental PXRD together with molecular structure as inputs to guide CSP from the outset. A multimodal neural network predicts probabilities for candidate space groups, which are then searched sequentially in descending probability order. Candidate structures are evaluated using PXRD agreement and relative energies, and the search terminates when a candidate satisfies the matching criterion. In a retrospective evaluation of 11 molecular-crystal systems, the protocol returned candidate sets containing structures matching the experimental crystal packing in nine cases. rubric.why: Directly MCSP-relevant and practical PXRD-guided pruning, but modest validation (9/11 systems) and an efficiency gain rather than new search or ranking SOTA.

summary: Multimodal network predicts space-group probabilities from experimental PXRD plus molecular graph; CSP then searches space groups sequentially by probability, terminating on PXRD/energy match, cutting cost versus 22-group exhaustive search.

title: Constrained Crystal Structure Prediction
abstract: Abstract The aim of first-principles crystal structure prediction (CSP) is computational identification of a compound’s experimentally isolable polymorph(s). The structure generation stage of CSP typically leads to hundreds of thousands of candidate structures across multiple space groups. However, in many use cases, experimental powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) data is available from high-throughput polymorph screening studies, but the crystal structure is not yet solved. For such cases, we propose using indexed lattice parameters to constrain the CSP search space. Searching only specific unit-cell dimensions allows a large reduction in the number of structures generated, whilst adding confidence that the experimental structure is retained in the search pool when advancing to density-functional reranking of the most likely candidates. Examples are shown for the cases of several small organic molecules, specifically uracil, paracetamol, progesterone, and four forms of the prolific polymorph-former, ROY. The accuracy of the constrained CSP (C-CSP) workflow is found to be highly dependent on the quality of the force field used for initial structure generation. Provided the force field

rubric.why: Directly MCSP and practically useful, but the idea of PXRD-constrained search is fairly incremental; success hinges on force-field quality, and the tests are small-scale.

summary: Uses indexed PXRD lattice parameters to constrain CSP structure generation to fixed unit cells, then DFT reranks; tested on uracil, paracetamol, progesterone and four ROY forms.

title: System of agentic AI for the discovery of metal–organic frameworks
abstract: Abstract Generative models and machine learning promise accelerated material discovery in metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) for CO 2 capture and water harvesting, but face substantial challenges in navigating vast chemical spaces while ensuring synthesizability. Here we present MOFGen, a system of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) comprising interconnected agents: a large language model that proposes MOF compositions, a diffusion model that generates crystal structures, quantum mechanical agents that optimize and filter candidates, and synthetic-feasibility agents guided by expert rules and machine learning. Trained on a broad set of experimentally reported MOFs and computational databases, MOFGen generated hundreds of thousands of MOF structures and synthesizable organic linkers. The uniqueness of our approach lies in its ability to generate large MOF structures with atomic precision, beyond the scale of conventional generative models limited to tens of atoms. This approach was validated through high-throughput experiments and the successful synthesis of four ‘AI-dreamt’ MOFs.

rubric.why: Experimental validation of generative crystal design is notable, but it is a system integration of existing components with no new theory; loosely relevant to crystal generation.

summary: Multi-agent pipeline (LLM composition proposer, diffusion structure generator, DFT filtering, synthesizability agents) generating large MOF crystal structures; four AI-generated MOFs experimentally synthesized.

title: Variational Monte Carlo for Quantum Excited States via Nested Low-Rank Approximation
abstract: The electronic Schrödinger equation encodes a molecule's electronic structure and quantum properties, but solving it scales exponentially with the number of electrons. Solving this equation with neural-network variational Monte Carlo (VMC) has reached chemical accuracy on the ground state of small molecules; extending this success to excited states is constrained by two existing paradigms. Penalty-based methods need $K$ Laplacians per step but require tuning the overlap-penalty weights against the energy gaps they aim to compute. Natural excited states VMC (NES-VMC) is penalty-free, but it combines the $K$ ansatzes into one determinant, whose local energy requires $K^2$ Laplacians per step. We resolve this trade-off via low-rank approximation (LoRA) reparameterization of the rank-$K$ variational objective. The reparameterized objective admits a VMC-compatible stochastic gradient estimator via MCMC sampling from the per-state Born densities, and a sequential nesting scheme recovers the lowest $K$ eigenstates in eigenvalue order.
